name: Ashwagandha

lead: Ashwagandha is a shrub whose root is a staple of Ayurvedic medicine, sold as an extract for stress, sleep and vitality. In fitness it is taken for better recovery, strength and testosterone support, with a more muscular, less stressed look as the goal.

Its withanolides appear to calm the stress axis, lower cortisol and affect GABA and inflammatory signalling, so any muscle effect comes through better stress, sleep and recovery rather than direct anabolism. Small randomized trials report modest gains in strength and some hormone readings, and meta-analyses report lower stress and anxiety scores. Visible appearance changes have not been studied directly.

paras: Taken daily as a root powder or standardized extract capsule, often in the evening, and stacked with sleep and recovery supplements. Trials run for weeks to a couple of months, and users usually notice stress and sleep changes before any training effect.

Sold as a supplement in most countries. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, and it can affect thyroid hormone levels and cause drowsiness or stomach upset. It is generally avoided in pregnancy and may interact with thyroid, sedative and immunosuppressant drugs.

angle.text: Ashwagandha is taken to lower stress, improve sleep and nudge testosterone, so you recover faster, train harder and build more muscle. Small human trials report modest changes in strength, stress scores and some hormone readings. Visible appearance changes have not been directly studied.

lead: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), also called Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is an evergreen shrub of the nightshade family whose root powder has been used for centuries in traditional Indian medicine [1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement as root or leaf powder or standardized extracts, marketed as an adaptogen for stress, sleep, vitality, strength and testosterone [1][2].

The main phytochemicals are withanolides, steroidal lactones such as withaferin A, which are structurally similar to ginsenosides, giving rise to the nickname 'Indian ginseng' [1]. In fitness communities it is used for recovery, stress and testosterone support, often alongside other herbal products [3][4].

Meta-analyses of randomised trials report reductions in stress and anxiety scores and a small effect on sleep, but with substantial heterogeneity [2][5][6]. Wikipedia states that current clinical evidence is insufficient to confirm safety or efficacy and notes rare cases of liver injury [1]. A few small trials have examined strength, recovery and endurance outcomes [7][8].
infobox: Avoid in pregnancy; reported rare liver injury [1]

paras: T Nation members list ashwagandha among stacks for stress, sleep and hormone support, including with tongkat ali and fadogia, in training logs, deployment supply lists and TRT recovery logs [3][4][9][10]. A forum post describes a social-media video promoting ashwagandha as a testosterone booster [11].
Ashwagandha root has been used for centuries in Indian traditional medicine [1]. Research has examined stress, anxiety, sleep, thyroid function, cognition and sexual health [2][5][6][12][13][14].

A 2022 meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (1,002 participants) found that ashwagandha reduced anxiety and stress scores compared with placebo, with very high heterogeneity [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of nine trials (558 patients) reported significant effects on the Perceived Stress Scale, Hamilton Anxiety Scale and serum cortisol, with mild to moderate adverse events in four trials [5].

A 2021 meta-analysis of five trials (400 participants) found a small but significant effect on sleep, more prominent in people with insomnia, at doses of at least 600 mg/day and for treatment of at least eight weeks [6]. A review of the endocrine system concluded that ashwagandha may have a positive effect on endocrine function but described the literature as heterogeneous [15].

For exercise, a 2015 randomised trial examined muscle strength and recovery with ashwagandha [7], and an 8-week randomised trial in people doing resistance training looked at endurance and VO2max [8]. A systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of ashwagandha and exercise performance has also been published [16]. Trials are small and several use proprietary standardised extracts; readers can consult each trial's funding statement.

Common side effects include diarrhea, headache, sedation and nausea [1]. Ashwagandha has been linked to herb-induced liver injury, particularly in people with preexisting liver conditions, and Wikipedia advises against use during pregnancy or in hormone-sensitive prostate cancer; it may raise testosterone, which could interact with cancer medications [1]. A pharmacological review discusses safety and toxicity aspects [17].

A T Nation user reported trying ashwagandha and not recommending it [18], another said it works best for them when cycled because it seems to lose effectiveness [10], and a third reported a testosterone rise after stopping an antioxidant containing ashwagandha, noting other possible explanations [19].

Withanolides are described as modulating the stress axis, lowering cortisol and affecting GABAergic and inflammatory signalling, according to reviews of its pharmacology [17][15]. Review articles also describe immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects, largely from preclinical work [17][20].
Ashwagandha has been used for over three thousand years in Indian systems of medicine, as a rasayana (rejuvenator), according to reviews [17][21].

Meta-analyses: stress and anxiety [2][5], sleep [6], exercise performance [16]. Randomised trials: a stress-relief trial of an extract [12], a standardised extract trial on stress hormones [22], subclinical hypothyroidism [23], qualitative analysis of a trial in college students [24], a 2015 trial on strength and recovery [7], and an 8-week resistance training trial on VO2max [8].

Registered trials include footballers' exercise performance (NCT06264986), muscle damage prevention (NCT06900569), adolescent football recovery (NCT07890935), sleep (NCT07151261), sexual health in men and women (NCT05840731, NCT05831241), college student stress (NCT05430685), cognition after chemotherapy (NCT04092647) and a root extract safety study (NCT06261476) [25][26][27][28][13][29][30][14][31].

lore.intro: On T Nation ashwagandha is mentioned mostly in supplement lists and TRT or stress threads, sometimes as a testosterone support and sometimes as a calming herb; experiences are mixed [3][18][10][10].
